html:
The Ojibwe, also called the Chippewa, are an Algonquian people of the upper Great Lakes, around Lake Superior. The map spells their name Obiwa. They call themselves Anishinaabe and their land Anishinabewaki.

By their own history they came west long ago from the Atlantic coast, following a sacred shell until they reached a land where food grows on water: wild rice. They fished, hunted, made maple sugar, and travelled by birchbark canoe. Their Midewiwin society kept sacred knowledge on birchbark scrolls. With the Odawa and Potawatomi they form the Council of Three Fires.

The Ojibwe were early allies of New France in the fur trade. With French guns they spread west and north in the 1700s, pushing the Dakota off the lakes of Minnesota, and onto the plains as the Plains Ojibwe. Today they are one of the largest Indigenous peoples of North America, with many reservations in the United States and reserves in Canada.
